hand-lettered grease-pencil slate whose keywords are legible frame by frame: "…HEADS"
(almost certainly BEACHHEADS), "AMMO", "HANDLING", "CLOTHES", "PARADE", and a
number "000627". So the footage is catalogued under *ammunition handling at a beachhead*.

The scene itself is an over-the-beach military resupply operation:

- A beached landing craft / LST-type vessel with its bow ramp down onto a causeway (2.7–15.5 s).
- The vessel's vehicle deck, a corridor running between two rows of parked armoured amphibians
  (15.5–25.7 s).
- A shore ammunition dump of stacked wooden crates stencilled "3 ROCKETS HE AT / 3.5 INCH M28A2
  / COMP B / LOT…" — 3.5-inch HEAT rocket ("super bazooka") ammunition (25.7–38.2 s).
- A loaded DUKW amphibious truck running in through the surf and up the beach, with a crowded
  anchorage of ships visible offshore in the haze (38.2–56.7 s).
- A US Army cargo truck sits at the shore end of the causeway; its white star insignia is clearly
  visible on the cab.

The clothing of the crowd (loose white and dark jackets, baggy trousers, headcloths, wide-brimmed
hats, rubber shoes), the carrying technique (loads balanced on the head), the American vehicles
and the 3.5-inch rocket crates together point to Korean War-era ship-to-shore logistics worked by
local civilian labour. The behavioural reading below does not depend on that identification, but
it is consistent with it.

## 2. The passage carries two opposed streams

Both "passages" — the causeway strip beside the beached craft, and the corridor down the ship's
vehicle deck — show the same pattern: two counter-flowing streams of people sharing one narrow
lane.

**The loaded stream.** Figures come down the ramp out of the ship and turn along the causeway
toward the waiting truck, each under a load: long white-painted wooden crates balanced flat on
the head, boxes hoisted on one shoulder, bundles and sacks carried high on the back. Their
posture is unmistakably that of burdened walking — neck and trunk braced, one or both hands up
steadying the box, short flat-footed steps, a slow and deliberate pace. Tracking individuals at
quarter-second intervals between 9.0 s and 10.25 s, and again between 16.2 s and 20.4 s on the
deck, shows them advancing steadily and continuously in one direction.

**The unloaded stream.** Simultaneously, other figures walk the other way — back along the
causeway and up the ramp into the ship — empty-handed, upright, arms swinging free, moving
visibly faster than the loaded stream. They are dressed identically to the carriers and pass them
shoulder to shoulder in the same lane. They are clearly visible at 9.0, 12.0 and 13.0 s with
their backs to the camera, heading toward the ramp.

At the dump (25.7–31.4 s) the same chain terminates: men arrive with crates high on their backs,
and pairs of men bend, lift and heave the boxes onto tiered stacks.

## 3. Are they all working, or are some supervising?

**Almost everyone visible is working. A very small number — one or two or three people in the
whole clip — are stationary at fixed posts rather than moving with the flow, and those are the
supervising/receiving element.**

I checked this rather than just eyeballing it. Averaging every frame of the causeway shot
together (6.3–15.5 s, ~285 frames) leaves moving people smeared into an unreadable blur but
leaves anyone who stood still sharp. In that average **exactly one human figure stays sharp: the
man standing in the bed of the star-marked truck.** Repeating the test over shorter 3-second
windows (at 6.3 s, 9.3 s and 12.3 s) confirms that *nobody else on the causeway holds still even
for three seconds* — every other person in shot is in continuous motion for the whole shot.

That gives a clean split:

- **The carriers — the overwhelming majority.** Civilian-dressed, many at once, strung out along
  the whole length of the passage in a continuous file. At any instant roughly a dozen to fifteen
  people are in frame, of whom typically four to six are visibly under a load.
- **The empty-handed people in the same file are also workers, not idlers or onlookers.** They are
  not loitering, watching, or standing about: they move purposefully in the return direction, they
  are dressed exactly like the carriers, and the two streams run continuously and in roughly
  balanced numbers. They are the same porters on the return leg, going back for the next box.
- **The genuine non-carriers.** The man in the truck bed wears a soft military-style field cap and
  light shirt. He never leaves the truck for the entire nine and a half seconds of the shot: he
  leans on the side rail looking down at the arriving line (6.3 s, 8.0 s, 11.4 s), then stoops out
  of sight to take and stow a load (9.7 s, 13.1 s, 14.8 s), then straightens and looks again. On
  the ship's vehicle deck, two figures in light shirts stand at the far (forward) end of the
  passage — where loads are being broken out of the stowed cargo — and hold essentially the same
  spot from 19.0 s through 25.0 s, upright and hands free, facing down the corridor while a
  procession of loaded porters files past below them.

Two honest qualifications. First, the man on the truck is not purely an overseer — he is visibly
handling cargo as well as watching, so his role is best described as receiving and stowing at a
control point rather than pure supervision. Second, at the ammunition dump (29.0–31.3 s) **both**
visible men are bent over lifting and stacking; there is no idle overseer standing in that shot at
all. So the supervisory layer here is genuinely thin — it is present, but it is a couple of people
at the interfaces, not a row of bosses watching a gang work.

## 4. What their movement implies

- **It implies a continuous hand-carry relay, not a one-off unloading or a disembarkation.** The
  defining signature is the steady counter-flow: loaded outbound, empty inbound, without a gap in
  either direction for the whole of both shots. The same people are cycling round and round
  between the ship's hold and the truck. If this were a group simply coming ashore, there would be
  only one direction of travel.
- **It implies the work is organised and directed, not spontaneous.** Two streams keep to a
  consistent route and a consistent handedness in a lane barely wide enough for both, and pass
  each other repeatedly without collision, bunching or milling about. Disciplined counter-flow in
  a congested space is a product of someone having allocated the route and the pace.
- **It implies the supervision is positioned at the chain's junctions, which is where it has to
  be.** The non-moving people are not scattered at random: they are precisely at the two points
  where the relay changes hands — the truck tailgate where loads leave the porters' shoulders, and
  the forward end of the deck where loads are issued. Their job is throughput control: metering
  the flow so the file neither starves nor jams.
- **It implies human muscle is substituting for machinery.** The cargo is being broken down into
  head- and shoulder-sized parcels and walked ashore rather than craned, netted or forklifted,
  which means the landing point has no port facilities — it is an unimproved beach with a causeway,
  which is also why DUKWs are ferrying loads through the surf in the closing shots.
- **It implies urgency.** Nobody rests, nobody stops on the route, the return leg is walked briskly
  rather than dawdled, and even the one stationary man is alternating between watching and lifting.
  A landing craft beached on a tidal shore has to be emptied and retracted quickly, and the tempo
  on screen matches that pressure.
- **It implies a division of labour along organisational lines.** The physical carrying is done by
  civilian-dressed labourers; the receiving and watching is done by the military-capped men at the
  vehicle and the light-shirted men at the cargo. That is a supply chain staffed at the bottom by
  hired or conscripted local porters and controlled at the top by the army that owns the cargo.
- **It implies the chain is actually delivering.** The crates coming down the passage are the same
  3.5-inch rocket boxes that appear a few shots later stacked in tiers ashore, with more being
  bedded into the pile by hand. The accumulating dump is the proof that the counter-flow is
  productive throughput rather than churn.

## 5. Short answer

They are not all doing the same job, but nearly all of them are working. The loaded people
carrying crates off the ship and the empty-handed people walking back the other way are the same
porters on opposite legs of one continuous shuttle — the returners are not idle, they are going
back for the next load, which is why they move faster and upright. Only a very small number of
people are not moving with the flow at all: a soldier standing in the bed of the army truck who
watches the arriving line and stoops to take each load, and one or two light-shirted figures who
hold station at the head of the ship's deck passage. Frame-averaging confirms that no one else on
the causeway stands still even for three seconds. So: a large working majority, with a thin
supervising/receiving layer stationed exactly at the chain's junctions. The movement as a whole
implies a deliberately organised, manpower-intensive, continuously cycling ship-to-shore
ammunition relay over an unimproved beach, run at speed under light but well-placed supervision.

## The two streams of people on the passage

**1. The carriers, moving from the ship to the truck.** Tracking individual people from frame to frame shows that every loaded person moves in the same direction: they come out of the ship at the top of the ramp, walk along it, and finish at the rear of the truck. Each carries one wooden ammunition crate balanced on the head or on one shoulder, steadied with one or both hands. They are civilian laborers in loose white or dark padded work clothes, several with cloth wound round the head as padding under the crate. New loaded carriers keep appearing at the ship end for the whole shot, so the supply of crates is continuous.

**2. The people moving the opposite way, from the truck back to the ship.** The figures walking back toward the ship are empty-handed. Their arms hang free or swing, there is nothing on their heads, and they wear exactly the same clothing as the carriers. They walk up the ramp and disappear into the ship, and the same kind of figure then re-emerges carrying a crate. They are the return leg of the same work gang going back for the next load, not people watching the work.

**Motion trace.** A time-versus-position trace of the ramp over about nine seconds shows the bright crate tracks all running ship-to-truck, and the dark tracks of people's bodies crossing in both directions in a repeating X pattern. There is no vertical (stationary) track of a person anywhere on the ramp itself: the only stationary marks are the ramp structure, the hoisting chain and the truck. Nobody in the moving line stops, gestures, points or turns to watch the others.

## Working or supervising?

**Everyone walking the passage, loaded or unloaded, is working.** The empty-handed walkers are not supervisors; they are laborers between loads. The cycle is: pick up a crate inside the ship, carry it down the ramp, hand it up onto the truck, walk back empty, repeat. The two directions are the two halves of a single loop, which is why the flow looks like a human conveyor belt and why the number of people coming back is roughly the same as the number going out.

**A small number of people are not part of that loop, and they are the ones who look like supervisors or overseers:**

- **A man in a military fatigue cap standing on the truck bed** at the foot of the ramp. Early in the shot he stands upright, looking back along the ramp at the approaching line. As crates arrive he bends and crouches inside the truck, taking each crate and stacking it. He stays fixed at one point instead of walking the circuit. He directs where the crates go and does the stacking himself, so he is part receiver, part overseer.
- **A second man in a visored cap and light shirt with a belt**, dressed differently from the laborers, hovers in the gap between the ramp foot and the truck from about 6 seconds onward. He drifts a little toward the truck, back toward the ramp, and toward the truck again while carriers stream past him, and around 13 to 14 seconds he walks to the truck with the loaded group. - **A figure in a long dark coat and cap** walks back toward the ship at roughly half the pace of the carriers, hands free apart from a small object. Most likely this is just a slow returning laborer, but the different dress and the slow, unhurried pace make a foreman a possibility.
- **On the ship's deck**, a person in a white shirt stands upright on top of the crate pile at the far end while others bend to hand crates down to the laborers, who then carry them toward the camera (toward the bow and ramp) while empty-handed men walk away from the camera back to the pile. The standing figure barely moves for several seconds and appears to be directing the break-out of the pile rather than lifting.
- **At the beach crate dump**, a man in a dark coat and cap waits at the stack, but as each carrier arrives he reaches out to take the crate and bends down to help set it in place, so there he is working alongside the carrier rather than only watching.

- **Two-way, non-stop traffic implies a repeating cycle, not a one-off transfer.** Loaded people go one way, empty people come back the other way, and loaded ones keep appearing from the ship. That is the signature of a gang shuttling between a source (the ship's cargo) and a destination (the truck), one crate per person per trip.
- **The direction of the loads shows this is unloading.** Crates travel only from the ship to the truck, and the truck is being filled by the man on its bed. The DUKWs coming ashore later fit the same picture: supplies are moving from the sea onto the beach.
- **Because everyone on the ramp keeps moving, no one on the ramp is supervising.** Supervision shows up as standing still, watching, pointing or checking, and the only people doing that are the few men in caps positioned at the ends of the passage (on the truck, in the gap at the ramp foot, on top of the deck pile), not in the moving line.
- **The work is manual and lightly overseen.** The unloading is done entirely by hand by civilian laborers, while a handful of uniformed men are placed at the receiving points to direct where the ammunition goes and to stack it. The division is clear: the many who move carry; the few who stay put oversee.

**In short:** the people carrying supplies and the people walking the opposite way are all working, because the ones walking back are simply returning empty for another crate; the two directions are one continuous loop. Only two or three men in caps, who stand at the ends of the passage or hover in it without ever carrying anything, appear to be supervising.
